table.text: We collected 549 surveys (M = 21.12, SD = 6.50, Median = 24.0 surveys per participant, 85% compliance). 4 The sampling scheme was signal-contingent with semi-random intervals, i.e., random signals were sent around fixed-time surveys. Participants received five notifications per day between 9 AM and 6 PM. The number of measurement occasions per day was selected based on previous work (e.g., Methot et al., 2021; Viererbl et al., 2022). At least 60 minutes were planned between consecutive notifications. Following the initial notification, each ESM questionnaire was available for 15 minutes. According to power heuristics for twolevel nested data (Arend and Schäfer, 2019), we can reliably detect within-person effect sizes, which our study aimed to target, of a minimum size of .19-.20 with this sample size.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Informal communication and well-being during work from home: Examining interaction effects with modality
table.description:
This preregistration is based on the (pre-)registration template for experience sampling methodology (ESM) research:

Kirtley, O. J., Lafit, G., Achterhof, R., Hiekkaranta, A. P., & Myin-Germeys, I. (2020, March 12). A template and tutorial for (pre-)registration of studies using Experience Sampling Methods (ESM). https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/2CHMU

An anonymized PDF version of this preregistration is attached to the project.

Study Information
1.	Title (required) 
Informal communication and well-being during work from home: Examining
interaction effects with modality

2.	Authors (required):
Author information are blinded for anonymous peer review. Authors will be identifiable after review via the non-anonymized OSF project link.


3.	Description (optional)
Around the globe, the COVID–19 pandemic led to a substantial increase in people working from home. These unique conditions when working from home also affect internal communication activities of organizations and especially informal communication processes among employees. While informal communication yields beneficial effects on employees’ resources and well-being, during work from home, it can mainly be conducted computer-mediated communication (CMC). In that way, informal communication via CMC may not yield the same benefits as face-to-face encounters, or it may even further deteriorate well-being. Whether this is truly the case, however, remains unclear. Thus, how informal CMC during work from home contributes to, or hampers, employees’ well-being, is of considerable interest to organizations and employees alike. The project will address this overarching question by drawing from interpersonal and informal communication literature, theory, as well as research on (mediated) social interactions and energy resources within the (remote) work domain to examine this question with a five-day experience sampling study among employees.

4.	Hypotheses (required)

H1: Within persons, informality of the communication episode will be positively associated with its striving potential at the situation level.

H2: Within persons, the striving potential of the informal communication episode will be positively associated with relatedness need satisfaction at the situation level.

H3: Within persons, the striving potential of the informal communication episode will be positively associated with social energy expenditure at the situation level.

H4: Within persons, relatedness need satisfaction during informal communication episodes will (a) be positively associated with vitality and (b) be negatively associated with fatigue at the end of the day.

H5: Within persons, social energy expenditure during informal communication episodes will (a) be negatively associated with vitality and (b) be positively associated with fatigue at the end of the day.

H6: Relatedness need satisfaction and social energy expenditure during informal communication episodes will interact within persons such that days with a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio than usual will (a) be positively associated with vitality and (b) be negatively associated with fatigue at the end of the day.

RQ1: How will the striving potential of the informal communication episode and modality interact in association to (a) relatedness need satisfaction and (b) social energy expenditure within persons at the situation level?

RQ2: Do the associations addressed in H1-H5 and RQ1 show between persons, as well?

Design Plan

5.	Study type (required)
Observational study
 

6.	Blinding (required for intervention studies)
Options are not applicable since the present study is not an intervention study. Please see question 7 below.

7.	Is there any additional blinding in this study? 
Participants are told the cover story that the study is about perceptions of flexwork models. Blinding is used to contain reactivity in responses during the ESM period.

8.	Study design (required)
This study’s design is an experience sampling design, i.e., a short term/intensive longitudinal design and consists of three parts:

Part 1 “Intake Survey”: The recruiting link will incorporate the intake survey hosted on SoSciSurvey (https://www.soscisurvey.de/en/index) which will be available seven days before the study period. This recruiting link will be accompanied by a posting on LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, or a personal message on WhatsApp. Participants will be recruited from the personal network of the author. Before filling out the intake, participants are informed about the procedure and duration of the study, the anonymized data collection as well as their withdrawal rights, and asked for their consent. The intake survey takes approx. seven minutes to complete. At the end of the intake, participants will be instructed about and guided to the ESM period and the ESM app movisensXS (https://www.movisens.com/en/products/movisensxs/) via a randomly displayed and personalized QR code created by movisens. 

Part 2 “ESM Period”: The ESM period lasts for 5 weekdays (Monday to Friday) per person. 

Part 3 “Exit Survey”: The exit survey hosted on SoSciSurvey will be available after the last end-of-day survey on day five of the ESM phase and will be accessible via the movisensXS messaging system via a personalized link. Participants are instructed to complete the exit survey until the following Sunday. The exit survey also incorporates a lottery as incentivization and the possibility to indicate whether participants would like to receive a summary of the results of the study. Finally, participants are thanked and debriefed. 
Sampling Plan

9.	Existing data (required)
Selected option: Registration prior to creation of data: As of the date of submission of this research plan for pre-registration, the data have not yet been collected, created, or realized. 

10.	Explanation of existing data (if applicable): N/A

11.	ESM data collection procedure (required) 
 
11.1.	Study duration (number of days)
The ESM period lasts for five weekdays (Monday to Friday) per person. The field phase in total is planned to last for 14 days (plans for prolonging the study duration, see section 14). Participants will be able to participate in one of two timeslots, each lasting a week. Those who complete the intake survey until Sunday evening before the first-week slot will participate in the ESM phase in the first-week slot, people who complete the intake during the first-week slot will be assigned to the second-week slot.
11.2.	Type of sampling scheme: 
The sampling scheme will be signal-contingent with semi-random intervals, i.e., random signals within fixed intervals. Participants receive six notifications per day between 9.30 AM and 7:30 PM on weekdays. The fixed intervals are distributed equally within this daily study period. There are at least 60 minutes between consecutive notifications. The last questionnaire of the day is an end-of-day survey that is available each day from 6 to 7:30 PM.

11.3.	Total number and type of items (open-ended or closed) and estimated questionnaire duration. The ESM-day questionnaire consists of 10-14 items and the end-of-day survey of 9-15 items. Questionnaire length varies as a function of certain item responses (e.g., some items are only presented after participants indicate that they are not on work duty and do not have had a social interaction in the last 60 minutes). Following a technical pilot, the completion time for each questionnaire is estimated to range from one to two minutes for each ESM assessment.

11.4.	Time-out specifications. 
Following the initial notification, each ESM questionnaire is available to the participant for 15 minutes.

11.5.	Additional passive monitoring. 
No additional passive monitoring is planned.

11.6.	Incentivization and increasing participant engagement. 
Participants are informed that they can participate in a lottery at the end of the exit survey. Participants can win one of four vouchers (worth 50 € each) optionally for an in Germany widely known store (otto.de) or another online store specialized for sustainable products (avocadostore.de). They are informed that only people who fill out the exit survey can get access to the lottery. Participants will not have access to their compliance information during the testing period. 
11.7.	Please indicate any additional details that are relevant to the ESM data collection procedure. N/A

12.	Sample size (number of participants) (required)
We aim to include at least 100 participants, preferably 120 participants, (level 2 units) in our sample.

13.	Rationale for sample size: Temporal design and number of participants (if applicable)
The minimum sample size for participants (level 2 units) is estimated based on previous ESM research in organizational psychology and communication (Fisher & To, 2012; Gabriel et al., 2019; Gilbert et al., 2021; Masur, 2019; Ohly et al., 2010; Schnauber-Stockmann & Karnowski, 2020; Vries et al., 2020). Due to time constraints of the sampling period and common compliance rates, sampling as many people as possible during this period is the central goal. The number of measurement occasions per day (level 1 units) is selected based on theoretical considerations in previous work (e.g., Methot et al., 2020) and results of a qualitative study from an unpublished student’s project on a similar topic. The number of study days per person is selected due to monetary constraints.

14.	Stopping rule (if applicable)
If compliance and participation rates are exceptionally low (e.g., far below 100 participants with completed intake, ESM, and exit surveys) after the planned two-week slots, the overall field phase may be prolonged for another week slot.
Variables

15.	Measured non-ESM/time-invariant variables (if applicable)

Intake-Survey:

Eligibility criteria.
Occupational Model (at least 20h of work per five days; based on Nübling et al., 2005)
Telework intensity in days per week (at least two days per week)
Age in years (at least 18 years old)
Use of Android phone

Job characteristics.
Occupational model (self-employed, employee, etc.; based on Nübling et al., 2005)
Number of occupations
Typical number of working days per week
Typical beginning and end time of work
Typical number of working hours per week (all occupations in total)
Shift work or very irregular shifts (Yes/No; Nübling et al., 2005)
Organizational tenure in years and months
Working industry (Destatis, 2010)
Characteristics of Work 4.0 (subscales flexibilization and delimination; Poethke et al., 2009)
Autonomy of private media use during work (adapted items from Gilbert et al., 2021; Sheldon & Hilpert, 2012)

Sociodemographics.
Size of household in number of persons
Number of kids in the main household
Gender
Highest level of Education

Exit Survey:

Self-reported compliance (based on Gilbert et al., 2021)
Typical working week. 

Additional measures relating to another project assessed in both Intake & Exit survey:
Meaning (Meaning presence subscale of the Meaning in Life Questionnaire; Steger et al., 2006)
Depression and Anxiety (Patient Health Questionnaire-4, PHQ-4, Löwe et al., 2010)
Social Support Provision (adapted from Social Support Inventory; Schwarzer, 1991)
Social Support Seeking (adapted from Social Support Inventory; Schwarzer, 1991)
Social Support Satisfaction (adapted from Social Support Inventory; Schwarzer, 1991)


16.	Measured ESM/time-variant variables (required)

ESM Day Survey:

Working context/on duty

Analysis Plan

Summary of the analysis plan: 
•	The data has a two-level structure, as repeated measurements (level 1) are nested within individuals (level 2). To account for the structure of the data, hypotheses relating to associations on the day level will be transformed by aggregating repeated measurements to day level by calculating a day-specific mean for each participant
•	For each hypothesis and RQ1, Random Effects Within Between (REWB) Models will be estimated/aimed at. Between-persons associations will be explored as part of the REWB models in the scope of RQ2.
•	All level 1 predictors (situational- and day level) will be centered around the person mean
•	All level 2 predictors (person level) will be centered around the sample’s grand mean.
•	Level 1 and level 2 controls will both be included in each model (since all models are REWB models) 

o	Control variables for models only referring to the situation level: age, gender, day of the week, hierarchy of interaction partners 
o	Control variables for models with end-of-day outcomes: age, gender, hierarchy of interaction partners, day of the week, daily working hours, daily job demands

•	Categorical variables will be dummy coded with a reference category that represents the most appropriate baseline level. In models with categorical variables of more than two values, there will be one reference category and, thus, three separate moderation analyses in the case of the modality variable that compare each value to the reference category.
•	The reporting of the analyses will be conducted according to the multilevel reporting guidelines by Luo et al. (2021)
•	Model specifications will be guided by the steps of Snijders & Bosker (2012) (see below)
•	The assumptions normal distribution, homoscedasticity, and linearity will be tested for each model
•	Active filters for the hypothesis 1-6 and RQ 1-2: 
o	Participants were on job duty during the last 60 minutes and work remotely
o	Participants had a social interaction during the last 60 minutes
o	Only for H2-6 and RQ1-2: Participants had an informal social interaction with colleagues or supervisors during the last 60 minutes (informality of the communication episode > 1)
•	For hypotheses incorporating two separate outcome variables, an equivalent model for each outcome will be estimated
•	Analysis software: R (certain steps of data wrangling may be done in SPSS), for multilevel modeling the lme4 package (Bates, 2015) will be used

 
20.	Statistical models (required)
20.1.	For each hypothesis and RQ1, Random Effects Within Between (REWB) models will be estimated/aimed at, since these are able to accord for level 1 and level 2 variance and allow to display varying between person intercepts and slopes (“keep it maximal“; Barr et al., 2013, see also Snijders & Bosker, 2012). Between-person associations will be explored as part of the REWB models in the scope of RQ2.

Model specifications will be guided by the steps outlined by Snijders & Bosker (2012, p. 158–167):
• Step 1: varying intercept model incl. calculation of the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)
• Step 2: Estimating a model with theoretically relevant L1 predictors and fixed slopes
o	Addition of predictor
o	Extending the model with control variables
• Step 3: Estimating a model with theoretically relevant L1 predictors and varying slopes
• Conclusive model comparison
o	Inspection of total fit-indices: Likelihood-Ratio-Test, AIC & BIC, Pseudo R²
o	If the model improves and there are no convergence issues, varying slopes will be kept
o	If the model does not improve with varying slopes or convergence issues emerge, slopes will be fixed again
• Step 4: Estimating a model with L1 predictors & fixed/varying slopes + theoretically relevant L2-predictors
• Step 5 (optional): Step 4 model + theoretically relevant interaction terms
o	Scenario 1: no significant interaction effect → only main effects will be interpreted 
o	Scenario 2: significant interaction effect → main & interaction effects will be interpreted as one system (Hox et al., 2018, p. 52)
• Step 6: Estimating all models with and without control variables, respectively
o	Model comparison with and without controls
o	Comparison of relevant model parameters (i.e., regression coefficients)
o	Robustness check: Do results of the hypotheses test stay the same if controls are included in the model?

23.1.	What criteria will you use to make inferences? Will you be using one or two-tailed tests for each of your analyses? If you are comparing multiple conditions or testing multiple hypotheses, will you account for this?
We will use a Likelihood ratio test to test the difference between two nested models using the Chi-squared distribution. 1.\tTitle (required)
Informal communication and well-being during work from home: Examining
interaction effects with modality

2.\tAuthors (required):
Author information are blinded for anonymous peer review. Authors will be identifiable after review via the non-anonymized OSF project link.


3.\tDescription (optional)
Around the globe, the COVID–19 pandemic led to a substantial increase in people working from home. These unique conditions when working from home also affect internal communication activities of organizations and especially informal communication processes among employees. While informal communication yields beneficial effects on employees’ resources and well-being, during work from home, it can mainly be conducted computer-mediated communication (CMC). In that way, informal communication via CMC may not yield the same benefits as face-to-face encounters, or it may even further deteriorate well-being. Whether this is truly the case, however, remains unclear. Thus, how informal CMC during work from home contributes to, or hampers, employees’ well-being, is of considerable interest to organizations and employees alike. The project will address this overarching question by drawing from interpersonal and informal communication literature, theory, as well as research on (mediated) social interactions and energy resources within the (remote) work domain to examine this question with a five-day experience sampling study among employees.

4.\tHypotheses (required)

H1: Within persons, informality of the communication episode will be positively associated with its striving potential at the situation level.

H2: Within persons, the striving potential of the informal communication episode will be positively associated with relatedness need satisfaction at the situation level.

H3: Within persons, the striving potential of the informal communication episode will be positively associated with social energy expenditure at the situation level.

H4: Within persons, relatedness need satisfaction during informal communication episodes will (a) be positively associated with vitality and (b) be negatively associated with fatigue at the end of the day.

H5: Within persons, social energy expenditure during informal communication episodes will (a) be negatively associated with vitality and (b) be positively associated with fatigue at the end of the day.

H6: Relatedness need satisfaction and social energy expenditure during informal communication episodes will interact within persons such that days with a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio than usual will (a) be positively associated with vitality and (b) be negatively associated with fatigue at the end of the day.

RQ1: How will the striving potential of the informal communication episode and modality interact in association to (a) relatedness need satisfaction and (b) social energy expenditure within persons at the situation level?

RQ2: Do the associations addressed in H1-H5 and RQ1 show between persons, as well?

8.\tStudy design (required)
This study’s design is an experience sampling design, i.e., a short term/intensive longitudinal design and consists of three parts:

Part 1 “Intake Survey”: The recruiting link will incorporate the intake survey hosted on SoSciSurvey (https://www.soscisurvey.de/en/index) which will be available seven days before the study period. This recruiting link will be accompanied by a posting on LinkedIn, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, or a personal message on WhatsApp. Participants will be recruited from the personal network of the author. Before filling out the intake, participants are informed about the procedure and duration of the study, the anonymized data collection as well as their withdrawal rights, and asked for their consent. The intake survey takes approx. seven minutes to complete. At the end of the intake, participants will be instructed about and guided to the ESM period and the ESM app movisensXS (https://www.movisens.com/en/products/movisensxs/) via a randomly displayed and personalized QR code created by movisens.

Part 2 “ESM Period”: The ESM period lasts for 5 weekdays (Monday to Friday) per person.

Part 3 “Exit Survey”: The exit survey hosted on SoSciSurvey will be available after the last end-of-day survey on day five of the ESM phase and will be accessible via the movisensXS messaging system via a personalized link. Participants are instructed to complete the exit survey until the following Sunday. The exit survey also incorporates a lottery as incentivization and the possibility to indicate whether participants would like to receive a summary of the results of the study. Finally, participants are thanked and debriefed.

11.\tESM data collection procedure (required)

11.1.\tStudy duration (number of days)
The ESM period lasts for five weekdays (Monday to Friday) per person. The field phase in total is planned to last for 14 days (plans for prolonging the study duration, see section 14). Participants will be able to participate in one of two timeslots, each lasting a week. Those who complete the intake survey until Sunday evening before the first-week slot will participate in the ESM phase in the first-week slot, people who complete the intake during the first-week slot will be assigned to the second-week slot.
11.2.\tType of sampling scheme:
The sampling scheme will be signal-contingent with semi-random intervals, i.e., random signals within fixed intervals. Participants receive six notifications per day between 9.30 AM and 7:30 PM on weekdays. The fixed intervals are distributed equally within this daily study period. There are at least 60 minutes between consecutive notifications. The last questionnaire of the day is an end-of-day survey that is available each day from 6 to 7:30 PM.

11.3.\tTotal number and type of items (open-ended or closed) and estimated questionnaire duration. The ESM-day questionnaire consists of 10-14 items and the end-of-day survey of 9-15 items. Questionnaire length varies as a function of certain item responses (e.g., some items are only presented after participants indicate that they are not on work duty and do not have had a social interaction in the last 60 minutes). Following a technical pilot, the completion time for each questionnaire is estimated to range from one to two minutes for each ESM assessment.

11.4.\tTime-out specifications.
Following the initial notification, each ESM questionnaire is available to the participant for 15 minutes.

11.5.\tAdditional passive monitoring.
No additional passive monitoring is planned.

11.6.\tIncentivization and increasing participant engagement.
Participants are informed that they can participate in a lottery at the end of the exit survey. Participants can win one of four vouchers (worth 50 € each) optionally for an in Germany widely known store (otto.de) or another online store specialized for sustainable products (avocadostore.de). They are informed that only people who fill out the exit survey can get access to the lottery. Participants will not have access to their compliance information during the testing period.

12.\tSample size (number of participants) (required)
We aim to include at least 100 participants, preferably 120 participants, (level 2 units) in our sample.

13.\tRationale for sample size: Temporal design and number of participants (if applicable)
The minimum sample size for participants (level 2 units) is estimated based on previous ESM research in organizational psychology and communication (Fisher & To, 2012; Gabriel et al., 2019; Gilbert et al., 2021; Masur, 2019; Ohly et al., 2010; Schnauber-Stockmann & Karnowski, 2020; Vries et al., 2020). Due to time constraints of the sampling period and common compliance rates, sampling as many people as possible during this period is the central goal. The number of measurement occasions per day (level 1 units) is selected based on theoretical considerations in previous work (e.g., Methot et al., 2020) and results of a qualitative study from an unpublished student’s project on a similar topic. The number of study days per person is selected due to monetary constraints.

If compliance and participation rates are exceptionally low (e.g., far below 100 participants with completed intake, ESM, and exit surveys) after the planned two-week slots, the overall field phase may be prolonged for another week slot.

Analysis Plan

Summary of the analysis plan:
•\tThe data has a two-level structure, as repeated measurements (level 1) are nested within individuals (level 2). To account for the structure of the data, hypotheses relating to associations on the day level will be transformed by aggregating repeated measurements to day level by calculating a day-specific mean for each participant
•\tFor each hypothesis and RQ1, Random Effects Within Between (REWB) Models will be estimated/aimed at. Between-persons associations will be explored as part of the REWB models in the scope of RQ2.
•\tAll level 1 predictors (situational- and day level) will be centered around the person mean
•\tAll level 2 predictors (person level) will be centered around the sample’s grand mean.
•\tLevel 1 and level 2 controls will both be included in each model (since all models are REWB models)

o\tControl variables for models only referring to the situation level: age, gender, day of the week, hierarchy of interaction partners
o\tControl variables for models with end-of-day outcomes: age, gender, hierarchy of interaction partners, day of the week, daily working hours, daily job demands

•\tCategorical variables will be dummy coded with a reference category that represents the most appropriate baseline level. In models with categorical variables of more than two values, there will be one reference category and, thus, three separate moderation analyses in the case of the modality variable that compare each value to the reference category.
•\tThe reporting of the analyses will be conducted according to the multilevel reporting guidelines by Luo et al. (2021)
•\tModel specifications will be guided by the steps of Snijders & Bosker (2012) (see below)
•\tThe assumptions normal distribution, homoscedasticity, and linearity will be tested for each model
•\tActive filters for the hypothesis 1-6 and RQ 1-2:
o\tParticipants were on job duty during the last 60 minutes and work remotely
o\tParticipants had a social interaction during the last 60 minutes
o\tOnly for H2-6 and RQ1-2: Participants had an informal social interaction with colleagues or supervisors during the last 60 minutes (informality of the communication episode > 1)
•\tFor hypotheses incorporating two separate outcome variables, an equivalent model for each outcome will be estimated
•\tAnalysis software: R (certain steps of data wrangling may be done in SPSS), for multilevel modeling the lme4 package (Bates, 2015) will be used


20.\tStatistical models (required)
20.1.\tFor each hypothesis and RQ1, Random Effects Within Between (REWB) models will be estimated/aimed at, since these are able to accord for level 1 and level 2 variance and allow to display varying between person intercepts and slopes (“keep it maximal“; Barr et al., 2013, see also Snijders & Bosker, 2012). Between-person associations will be explored as part of the REWB models in the scope of RQ2.

Model specifications will be guided by the steps outlined by Snijders & Bosker (2012, p. 158–167):
• Step 1: varying intercept model incl. calculation of the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)
• Step 2: Estimating a model with theoretically relevant L1 predictors and fixed slopes
o\tAddition of predictor
o\tExtending the model with control variables
• Step 3: Estimating a model with theoretically relevant L1 predictors and varying slopes
• Conclusive model comparison
o\tInspection of total fit-indices: Likelihood-Ratio-Test, AIC & BIC, Pseudo R²
o\tIf the model improves and there are no convergence issues, varying slopes will be kept
o\tIf the model does not improve with varying slopes or convergence issues emerge, slopes will be fixed again
• Step 4: Estimating a model with L1 predictors & fixed/varying slopes + theoretically relevant L2-predictors
• Step 5 (optional): Step 4 model + theoretically relevant interaction terms
o\tScenario 1: no significant interaction effect → only main effects will be interpreted
o\tScenario 2: significant interaction effect → main & interaction effects will be interpreted as one system (Hox et al., 2018, p. 52)
• Step 6: Estimating all models with and without control variables, respectively
o\tModel comparison with and without controls
o\tComparison of relevant model parameters (i.e., regression coefficients)
o\tRobustness check: Do results of the hypotheses test stay the same if controls are included in the model?

23.\tInference criteria (if applicable)
23.1.\tWhat criteria will you use to make inferences? Please describe the information you will use (e.g. p-values, Bayes factors, specific model fit indices), as well as the cut-off criterion, where appropriate. Will you be using one or two-tailed tests for each of your analyses? If you are comparing multiple conditions or testing multiple hypotheses, will you account for this?
We will use a Likelihood ratio test to test the difference between two nested models using the Chi-squared distribution. Confidence intervals and p-values will be reported transparently to make inferences along with effect size parameters of the likelihood ratio test. P-values will be interpreted as significant at the standard p < .05 threshold. Explained variation will be reported with a pseudo R2 (Snijders & Bosker, 2012; Xu, 2003). For each analysis, two-tailed tests will be used. In addition, further common model fit indices beyond the likelihood ratio (e.g., AIC, BIC) will be taken into consideration for model comparisons.

•\tBased on the latter and similar studies in communication and organizational psychology, a compliance rate of 60 percent or above is expected (de Vries et al., 2020; Ohly et al., 2010; Schnauber-Stockmann & Karnowski, 2020)

25.\tData exclusion (if applicable)
25.1.\tIrrespective of whether data are pre-existing, will participants or observations be excluded based upon missingness, due to either technical issues or compliance? If so, specify a decision rule for this including:
25.1.1.\tHow will you define a valid observation?
All completed ESM-observations will be defined as valid (for exceptions see section 25.2) since the movisensXS app asks participants with an alarm to continue or dismiss a survey every 1-2 minutes the survey is opened but not completed. If participants indicate they want to drop out of the study, their data will be deleted and excluded from the analysis.
All intake surveys completed within 1-30 minutes will be defined as valid. All completed exit surveys will be defined as valid.
25.1.2.\tHow will you define compliance? E.g., Will notifications missing due to technical problems be counted as non-compliance? Will you use information regarding valid responses to determine compliance? In case you set a minimum compliance rate or threshold for each participant, please specify the value or range that you will use in the analysis and provide a justification for this.
Compliance will be defined as the number of all valid notifications divided by the total number of delivered notifications. If a participant experiences technical issues, compliance will be calculated based on episodes when technical issues were not present.
25.2.\tWhich criteria will you use to define an outlier? How will outliers be handled? How are you going to deal with careless responding?
Outliers for the following independent and dependent variables will be examined: Informality of the Communication Episode, Striving Potential of the Communication Episode, Relatedness Need Satisfaction, Social Energy Expenditure, State Vitality, and State Fatigue. Outliers are defined as a score of ± 3 SDs from the grand mean on the mentioned variables. Sensitivity analysis using boxplots will be conducted and the overall confirmatory analyses will be run with and without outliers.

Careless responding will be dealt with the following procedure:
•\tIf completion of the full intake survey occurs in less than 1 minute, cases will be excluded from the analysis
•\tIf completion of an ESM survey occurs in less than 20 seconds, the ESM case will be set to NA
•\tIntake surveys with a variance of zero on at least three continuous measures will be excluded from the analysis.
•\tESM surveys with a variance of zero on all continuous measures will be set to NA

26.\tExploratory analysis (if applicable)
If H1 has to be rejected, associations of Informality of the Communication Episode and the variables Striving Potential, (b) Relatedness Need Satisfaction, or (c) Social Energy Expenditure will be explored dependent on different cut-offs between the scale’s extremes ‘completely formal’ and ‘completely informal’. Additionally, a within/between correlation matrix will be calculated. Further exploratory analyses will be labeled transparently as ‘not preregistered’.

#### Careless Responding

8 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **8 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).

live_data_statements: Twenty-six adult German-speaking employees (Mage = 32.40, SDage = 11.20, 61.5% female, 88.46% highly educated, 69.2% white-collar workers) were recruited between November and the beginning of December 2021 via convenience samplingfoot_2 .
Participants had to work at least 20 hours during the week, including at least two days of work from home, and use an Android phone to access the ESM app movisensXS.
Participants were told the cover story that the study is about perceptions of flex work models.
Before completion, participants were informed about the study procedure and asked to provide their consent.
At the end of the intake, participants were instructed about and guided to the ESM app movisensXS via a personalized link (n = 55 onboardings).

The ESM survey (M = 52.40, SD = 50.60 in seconds) measured the following constructs: Participants were first asked where they had worked during the last 60 minutes (in-office, at home, or at another place outside an office, not on duty or available to co-workers).
Next, participants were asked whether they had a conversation with their co-workers or supervisors during this time, as a filter question (Hall, 2018).
Participants were then requested to indicate whether certain attributes on five continua applied to their referred conversation (Likert-type scale from -3 to +3) (Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 33).

Using measures from the Rochester Interaction Record (Reis and Wheeler, 1991), participants were asked if they found the referred conversation "superficial" vs. "deep", "meaningless" vs. "meaningful", "unpleasant" vs. "pleasant", "impersonal" vs. "personal", and whether they "disclosed very little" vs. "a great deal" on the 7-point semantic differential scale, reflecting low vs. high striving potential.

For instance, participants were asked on which hierarchy level the people they had the conversation with were mostly (single-choice question; options: lower, similar, higher, or different hierarchy levels).

All models were "kept maximal" (Barr et al., 2013), meaning that intercepts and slopes between participants were allowed to vary if the model converged, and that models contained within-and between-predictors and moderators.

For interpersonal and organizational researchers as well as CMC scholars, this study extends CBB Theory by investigating part of its proposed mechanisms in a hybrid work context, where participants are also sometimes obliged to communicate more or less than preferred (Hall, 2018; Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 2 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Purpose: Informal communication has been ascribed well-being functions.

Yet in increasingly hybrid work settings, where employees work remotely, informal exchanges frequently occur via digital channels and may hinder relational bonds and drain rather than restore employees' energy.

Drawing on Communicate Bond Belong Theory, this study examines whether informal communication enhances or undermines employees' well-being in hybrid settings by considering its perceived quality, relational benefits, and energy-related costs.
Design/methodology/approach: A one-week experience sampling study (26 participants; 549 surveys) captured employees' everyday communication episodes with co-workers and their subsequent experiences.
Mixed-effects models estimated within-person relationships while accounting for between-person differences.
Findings: Episodes that were more informal than usual were associated with higher striving potential (e.g., more pleasantness or meaningfulness).
In turn, higher striving potential was associated with more relatedness need satisfaction and a more favorable relatedness-to-energy ratio, though not with energy expenditure.
Communication modality did not moderate these associations.
However, text-based (vs. audio-visual) exchanges were significantly associated with lower relatedness and energy expenditure, and a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio.
Originality: Adopting a situational perspective, this study moves beyond frequency-based and between-person approaches to everyday informal communication.
It disentangles message-and channel-related effects and their distinct contributions in the relationship between informal talk and employee well-being.

From this novel perspective, the findings provide evidence that informal communication is a resource for employees' well-being, but can impose demands when it occurs digitally, an aspect that practitioners should recognize when designing informal communication initiatives.
informal episode may not relate to well-being the same way across modalities.
Given this importance of different modalities for well-being in hybrid work, we ask: How does informal communication in hybrid work contribute to, or hamper, employees' well-being?
We address this question by drawing on Hall and Davis' (2017) Communicate Bond Belong (CBB) Theory to explain how informal social interactions can promote well-being.

text.text: Based on CBB Theory, we study informal interactions and well-being through a situational lens, focusing on the quality, relational benefits, and energy-resource drawbacks of communication episodes, while also examining their modality in each encounter.
A preregistered study using the experience sampling method (Beal, 2015) investigates the proposed associations in daily work life.

text.text: We specify the mechanism through which informal communication supports well-being, refining this understanding by disentangling the contribution of the communication itself from that of the modality through which it occurs.
A common way to describe internal communication is to differentiate between its formal and informal characteristics (Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990).

Informal communication is interpersonal talk occurring in an organizational setting between members of the organization itself (Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017).

Content.

Informal conversations have been identified as coming in various, often conceptually overlapping 'faces', such as rumor or grapevine (Crampton et al., 1998), humor or joking around (Winslow et al., 2019), small talk (Holmes, 2003), or as a specific subform like gossip (i.e., talking informally about a person not part of the conversation; Sun et al., 2023).

text.text: These faces and themes imply that informal communication arises from employees' psychological needs for exchange rather than extrinsically imposed task demands.
Informal communication used to be an activity that occurred primarily or exclusively face-to-face, as it is largely fostered by proximity (Mandhana, 2024; Whittaker et al., 1994).

text.text: Yet, nowadays, many employees can be "permanently connected" to co-workers via digital technology and mobile devices during both work and non-work time (Sonnentag, 2017).

text.text: Informal communication in hybrid work settings, therefore, often occurs as computer-mediated communication (CMC), defined as "multimodal human-to-human social interaction mediated by information and communication technologies" (Meier and Reinecke, 2021, p. 1183) via private or group chats of varying modality (Begemann et al., 2024; Viererbl et al., 2021).

text.text: Situation.

Most informal conversations take place at the office as a morning chat or during lunch breaks (Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017; Crampton et al., 1998), often alongside formal, scheduled meetings (e.g., "pre-meeting talk"; Allen et al., 2014), or sometimes as part of organizational etiquette or social rituals (Methot et al., 2021).

text.text: Again, a core definitional challenge is that informal communication appears fragmented throughout conversations among employees (Whittaker et al., 1994): a conversation may, for instance, start informally but then move on to a formal matter, such as pre-meeting talk (Allen et al., 2014).

text.text: Because of this fragmentation, the distinction between formal and informal communication is a continuum stretching from formal to informal interactions (Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990), making informality a matter of degree, varying with the extent to which an episode is intrinsically driven rather than externally demanded, as perceived by the communicator.

text.text: We locate the distinction in individuals' momentary intrinsic, relational needs for belonging and (professional) relationship building and maintenance, and within a subjective appraisal of the encounter (cf., Methot et al., 2026).

text.text: We define informal communication as all interpersonal and group communication activities within an organization that are, to varying degrees, driven by employees' momentary intrinsic needs related to relationship formation or strengthening, rather than by extrinsic demands.

This definition holds even when the interaction serves work-related ends as a byproduct or if the perception of informality differs between communicators, refining previous role-and goal-based definitions (Koch and Denner, 2022).
text.formatted: This definition holds even when the interaction serves work-related ends as a byproduct or if the perception of informality differs between communicators, refining previous role-and goal-based definitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Koch and Denner, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The frequency, structure, and classification of informal communication are themselves shaped by boundary conditions.
They can be affected by the channel (i.e., face-to-face vs.
CMC), the communicators' characteristics, the content (e.g., private vs. non-private), and the situation (e.g., in-office vs. remote).
These contingencies could both affect the benefits and costs of informal communication for well-being in hybrid work settings.
Although the many faces of informal communication are often of interest, the qualities of the respective encounters are rarely measured.

Scholars commonly assess social interaction or informal communication frequency (e.g., Denner et al., 2025; Van Zoonen and Sivunen, 2022), objective proximity (e.g., Mandhana, 2024), or app use (e.g., Carramenha et al., 2019), mostly between individuals.

text.text: Such proxies register the mere occurrence of communication or its boundary conditions, e.g., channel or context (Singh and Denner, 2025), rather than the social qualities that give communication its bearing on well-being.

text.text: Instead, an interpersonal communication perspective, one that researches the form and qualities of social interactions in dyads or small groups and investigates different communication occurrences within individuals, can overcome these limitations.

It shifts the unit of analysis from a person's general tendencies to communication episodes such as catching up, chit-chat, or meaningful talk during everyday work life (Goldsmith and Baxter, 1996; Hall and Davis, 2017; Ledbetter et al., 2011).

text.text: According to Hall (2018), communication episodes "represent the link between internal relational perceptions and manifest social behavior" (p. 4), each carrying its own relational benefits and social costs.

text.text: They are thus a meaningful unit of analysis to study the different 'faces' of informal communication, such as small talk (Methot et al., 2021) or joking around (Winslow et al., 2019), across channels, communicators, and situations.

text.text: Building on this interpersonal and situational view on communication, Hall and Davis' (2017) Communicate Bond Belong (CBB) Theory explains how and under which conditions different types of social interactions can lead to well-being and considers situational communication episodes as the central units of analysis.
According to CBB Theory, social interaction episodes have the potential to satiate humans' intrinsic need to belong, i.e., helping humans to form and strengthen relationships with others.
Feelings of relatedness, then, are the sought-after outcome of communicative behaviour and serve as a proxy for the need to belong being satisfied at a given time (Hall and Davis, 2017).
text.formatted: Feelings of relatedness, then, are the sought-after outcome of communicative behaviour and serve as a proxy for the need to belong being satisfied at a given time <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hall and Davis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, all communication episodes typically expend energy resources (Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 38).
text.formatted: However, all communication episodes typically expend energy resources <ref type="bibr">(Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 38)</ref>.

text.text: This creates a cost-benefit relationship between social benefits and energy-related drawbacks of any daily life social interaction.
Specifically, some types of social interactions, called striving episodes, can make a particularly significant contribution to well-being by potentially satiating the need to belong more than others.
Episodes that enhance bond formation or strengthening are assumed to qualify as striving behaviour.

Social interactions that convey increased affection, meaningfulness, pleasantness, or self-disclosure have been classified as potentially striving, whereas, conversely, superficial, unpleasant, and impersonal interactions have been classified as potentially less striving (Hall, 2018, p. 16; Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 33).
text.formatted: Social interactions that convey increased affection, meaningfulness, pleasantness, or self-disclosure have been classified as potentially striving, whereas, conversely, superficial, unpleasant, and impersonal interactions have been classified as potentially less striving <ref type="bibr">(Hall, 2018, p. 16;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 33)</ref>.

text.text: CBB Theory thus suggests a negative association between episode frequency and the likelihood of being a striving behaviour (Hall, 2018; Hall and Davis, 2017).
text.formatted: CBB Theory thus suggests a negative association between episode frequency and the likelihood of being a striving behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hall and Davis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, humans seem to engage less frequently in communication with striving qualities than in other kinds of interpersonal talk.
The authors reason this with communication episodes varying by required attention and effort (Hall, 2018) and with social interaction operating within a selfregulatory system.
text.formatted: The authors reason this with communication episodes varying by required attention and effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall, 2018)</ref> and with social interaction operating within a selfregulatory system.

text.text: Specifically, because humans have a finite amount of social energy, they generally try to conserve it when possible.

Hence, a high need-fulfilling potential and low energy expenditure should be the preferable type of interaction for individuals (Hall, 2018; Hall and Davis, 2017), particularly at work, where their communication activities are shaped by obligations and routines.
text.formatted: Hence, a high need-fulfilling potential and low energy expenditure should be the preferable type of interaction for individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hall and Davis, 2017)</ref>, particularly at work, where their communication activities are shaped by obligations and routines.

text.text: Based on CBB Theory, informal communication should thus contribute to well-being if it comes in a shape that (a) bears high striving potential and (b) cultivates more relatedness than expending social energy.

According to the circumplex model (Methot et al., 2026), informal communication varies by interaction quality relevant to relational need satisfaction, and can be enriching but also awkward, impersonal, or exhausting at other times.
text.formatted: According to the circumplex model <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Methot et al., 2026)</ref>, informal communication varies by interaction quality relevant to relational need satisfaction, and can be enriching but also awkward, impersonal, or exhausting at other times.

text.text: We therefore treat informal communication as a potentially need-satisfying form of interaction, as any single episode may be appraised as rewarding or aversive.
Yet its average striving potential should be positive for two reasons.
First, an appraisal of a communication episode can be positive regardless of an episode's 'face'.
Grounded in the need to belong (Baumeister and Leary, 1995), social contact is intrinsically rewarding because it signals connection.
text.formatted: Grounded in the need to belong <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Baumeister and Leary, 1995)</ref>, social contact is intrinsically rewarding because it signals connection.

text.text: This underlies the core function of informal communication in developing relationships and a sense of belonging at work (e.g., Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017; Denner et al., 2025; Fay, 2011; Kim et al., 2017; Methot et al., 2026; Winslow et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This underlies the core function of informal communication in developing relationships and a sense of belonging at work (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bielenia-Grajewska, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Denner et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Fay, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kim et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Methot et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Winslow et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Even routine small talk that appears mundane can elevate belonging (Hall et al., 2021; Methot et al., 2021; Sandstrom and Dunn, 2014), and even normatively negative talk, such as gossip (Sun et al., 2023), can be pleasant or meaningful to the communicator.
text.formatted: Even routine small talk that appears mundane can elevate belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hall et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Methot et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Sandstrom and Dunn, 2014)</ref>, and even normatively negative talk, such as gossip <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Sun et al., 2023)</ref>, can be pleasant or meaningful to the communicator.

text.text: Second, because informal communication is, by our definition, more intrinsically motivated than obligatory, employees tend to exercise greater volition over when and with whom they engage in it.
This selfselection should increase experienced quality, as people gravitate toward need-fulfilling and away from need-frustrating contact (Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017).
text.formatted: This selfselection should increase experienced quality, as people gravitate toward need-fulfilling and away from need-frustrating contact <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hall et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hall and Davis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Even where complete avoidance is difficult at work, individuals retain more autonomy in informal than formal interactions.
In addition, many workplace ties take the form of "fringeships" (Fingerman et al., 2025): ties between weak and close ones, marked by mutual affection, positive in tone, and volitional in nature.
text.formatted: In addition, many workplace ties take the form of "fringeships" <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Fingerman et al., 2025)</ref>: ties between weak and close ones, marked by mutual affection, positive in tone, and volitional in nature.

text.text: These fringeships are common for work relationships and are a context in which informal communication is especially likely to be appraised as relationally rewarding.

Since we understand informal communication as varying on a continuum between being completely informal and completely formal (Koch and Denner, 2022; Kraut et al., 1990), we conceptualize the degree of 'informality' as a continuous characteristic of communication episodes.
text.formatted: Since we understand informal communication as varying on a continuum between being completely informal and completely formal <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Koch and Denner, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kraut et al., 1990)</ref>, we conceptualize the degree of 'informality' as a continuous characteristic of communication episodes.

text.text: This characteristic lies at the situation level, varying from interaction to interaction.

Besides communication quality, informal communication should contribute to well-being if it cultivates relatedness, because feelings of relatedness are a proxy for satiating the need to belong in the present moment (Hall et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Besides communication quality, informal communication should contribute to well-being if it cultivates relatedness, because feelings of relatedness are a proxy for satiating the need to belong in the present moment <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hall et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: By establishing social bonds, providing social support among co-workers, and buffering employees' stress responses (Denner et al., 2025), these striving episodes should be positively associated with feelings of relatedness, well captured by relatedness need satisfaction (Ryan and Deci, 2000).
text.formatted: By establishing social bonds, providing social support among co-workers, and buffering employees' stress responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Denner et al., 2025)</ref>, these striving episodes should be positively associated with feelings of relatedness, well captured by relatedness need satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Ryan and Deci, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, Hall and Davis (2017) propose that all communication episodes typically expend energy.
text.formatted: Additionally, <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hall and Davis (2017)</ref> propose that all communication episodes typically expend energy.

text.text: Episodes with a higher striving potential have been shown to occur to a lesser extent than non-striving episodes as they should require more attention and involvement (Hall, 2018) and should therefore be more depleting than episodes with less striving potential.
text.formatted: Episodes with a higher striving potential have been shown to occur to a lesser extent than non-striving episodes as they should require more attention and involvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall, 2018)</ref> and should therefore be more depleting than episodes with less striving potential.

text.text: Hence, drawing on CBB Theory's premises, the present study argues that while cultivating relatedness, episodes with higher striving potential should also expend higher social energy as a second outcome characteristic of striving episodes.

Finally, the cost-benefit view rooted in CBB Theory holds that informal conversation enhances well-being when its relational benefits outweigh its energy costs, a balance captured by the relatedness-to-energy ratio (Hall, 2018; Hall and Merolla, 2020).
text.formatted: Finally, the cost-benefit view rooted in CBB Theory holds that informal conversation enhances well-being when its relational benefits outweigh its energy costs, a balance captured by the relatedness-to-energy ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hall and Merolla, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We expect striving episodes to yield a higher ratio.
First, as argued above, they are appraised as more relationally rewarding, raising the relatedness benefit.

Second, much striving talk is low in energetic cost: grounded in CBB Theory's energy-conservation principle, routine and familiar interactions become less effortful over time (Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017).
text.formatted: Second, much striving talk is low in energetic cost: grounded in CBB Theory's energy-conservation principle, routine and familiar interactions become less effortful over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hall et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hall and Davis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Informal striving episodes are also highly recurrent in everyday work life, where their regularity makes each instance comparatively low-cost while still delivering relational benefit (Methot et al., 2021; Winslow et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Informal striving episodes are also highly recurrent in everyday work life, where their regularity makes each instance comparatively low-cost while still delivering relational benefit <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Methot et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Winslow et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Striving episodes should thus raise relatedness without a commensurate rise in energy expenditure, consistent with Hall's (2018) finding that episodes such as joking around and expressing affection are high in the relatedness-to-energy ratio.
text.formatted: Striving episodes should thus raise relatedness without a commensurate rise in energy expenditure, consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hall's (2018)</ref> finding that episodes such as joking around and expressing affection are high in the relatedness-to-energy ratio.

text.text: When working remotely, not only the attributes of a communication episode but also its channel characteristics matter, as digital affordances are assumed to shape how media influence the relational and well-being outcomes of communication (Evans et al., 2017).
text.formatted: When working remotely, not only the attributes of a communication episode but also its channel characteristics matter, as digital affordances are assumed to shape how media influence the relational and well-being outcomes of communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Evans et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To understand how channel shapes communication, scholars highlight modality, which describes "how messages are delivered or presented via a medium.
For example, text, graphics, sound, and video" (Bracken and Dalessandro, 2017, p. 2; Meier and Reinecke, 2021).
text.formatted: For example, text, graphics, sound, and video" <ref type="bibr">(Bracken and Dalessandro, 2017, p. 2;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Meier and Reinecke, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Modality may shape a communication episode's consequences in interaction with its communicative qualities, such that the same informal exchange can yield different relational and energetic outcomes depending on how it is mediated.
It thus bears on the outcomes CBB Theory identifies: relatedness, energy expenditure, and their trade-off.
Striving potential reflects the relational properties of a communication episode and is the baseline driver of its outcomes.
More striving-laden talk should more strongly satisfy the need to belong, increasing relatedness, but it is also effortful and draws on energetic resources (Hall and Davis, 2017).
text.formatted: More striving-laden talk should more strongly satisfy the need to belong, increasing relatedness, but it is also effortful and draws on energetic resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hall and Davis, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Modality may modulate each of these relationships in different ways.
For relatedness, modality may work in opposing directions.

Leaner channels convey fewer verbal and nonverbal cues, which theories from the cues-filtered-out paradigm in CMC (e.g., Media Richness; Daft and Lengel, 1986) suggest may weaken the relatedness a communication episode with striving characteristics would typically convey.
text.formatted: Leaner channels convey fewer verbal and nonverbal cues, which theories from the cues-filtered-out paradigm in CMC (e.g., Media Richness; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Daft and Lengel, 1986)</ref> suggest may weaken the relatedness a communication episode with striving characteristics would typically convey.

text.text: Yet because remote informal communication is often more intentional, and occurs as scheduled and planned events, it skews toward the volitional, chosen episodes that CBB Theory links to greater relatedness (Hall et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Yet because remote informal communication is often more intentional, and occurs as scheduled and planned events, it skews toward the volitional, chosen episodes that CBB Theory links to greater relatedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hall et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, these episodes often happen with a narrower network of close ties, which would draw the relatedness upwards again (Begemann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In addition, these episodes often happen with a narrower network of close ties, which would draw the relatedness upwards again <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Begemann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Whether modality raises or lowers the relatedness derived from striving is therefore unclear.
For energy expenditure, mediated communication may amplify the costs.

Because remote informal communication must be deliberately enacted, employees must decide whether and how to initiate contact and which channel to use, which presents an effort preceding the exchange (Begemann et al., 2024; Viererbl et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Because remote informal communication must be deliberately enacted, employees must decide whether and how to initiate contact and which channel to use, which presents an effort preceding the exchange <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Begemann et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Viererbl et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The exchange itself then imposes processing demands that rise with modality richness: cue-rich media such as video require sustained cognitive resources ("Zoom fatigue"; Bailenson, 2021), while text also taxes resources, albeit to a lesser extent.
text.formatted: The exchange itself then imposes processing demands that rise with modality richness: cue-rich media such as video require sustained cognitive resources ("Zoom fatigue"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bailenson, 2021)</ref>, while text also taxes resources, albeit to a lesser extent.

text.text: As digital informal communication typically occurs simultaneously to other activities (Begemann et al., 2024), demands should also be higher due to task-switching or multitasking.
text.formatted: As digital informal communication typically occurs simultaneously to other activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Begemann et al., 2024)</ref>, demands should also be higher due to task-switching or multitasking.

text.text: Because modality may raise the cost of communicating, either through enactment effort, processing demands, or both, while its effect on relatedness remains uncertain, its net consequence for the relatedness-to-energy balance remains an open question.
We therefore investigate how modality and the striving potential are associated with relatedness, energy expenditure, and their ratio.
To match the situational and episodic focus of social interaction at work, an experience sampling study was conducted.

The experience sampling method (ESM) is an intensive longitudinal design, widely used in organizational research, that includes multiple self-report measures per day to capture individuals' lived, day-to-day experience (Beal, 2015).foot_1

text.text: Twenty-six adult German-speaking employees (Mage = 32.40, SDage = 11.20, 61.5% female, 88.46% highly educated, 69.2% white-collar workers) were recruited between November and the beginning of December 2021 via convenience samplingfoot_2 .
text.formatted: Twenty-six adult German-speaking employees (Mage = 32.40, SDage = 11.20, 61.5% female, 88.46% highly educated, 69.2% white-collar workers) were recruited between November and the beginning of December 2021 via convenience sampling<ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">foot_2</ref> .

text.text: During this period, COVID-19 restrictions had eased relative to earlier lockdowns, with most participants alternating between home and office within the same week and retaining in-person social contact, conditions closer to contemporary hybrid work than to lockdown.
Participants had to work at least 20 hours during the week, including at least two days of work from home, and use an Android phone to access the ESM app movisensXS.
Participants were told the cover story that the study is about perceptions of flex work models.
They could participate in a lottery at the end of the study period and were able to win one of four gift cards (worth 50 € each).
The study consisted of (a) an intake survey, (b) an experience sampling assessment period, and (c) an exit survey: The recruitment link incorporated the intake survey hosted on SoSciSurvey (n = 72).
Before completion, participants were informed about the study procedure and asked to provide their consent.
At the end of the intake, participants were instructed about and guided to the ESM app movisensXS via a personalized link (n = 55 onboardings).
On the following Monday, the ESM period lasted from Monday to Friday (n = 35 ESM participants).
The exit survey, hosted on SoSciSurvey, was available after the last prompted survey on day five of the ESM period.
The exit survey (n = 31) included the incentivization and a debriefing.

We collected 549 surveys (M = 21.12, SD = 6.50, Median = 24.0 surveys per participant, 85% compliance). 4 The sampling scheme was signal-contingent with semi-random intervals, i.e., random signals were sent around fixed-time surveys.

text.text: As a prerequisite for multilevel modeling, the ICCs of all situational variables were inspected.
For all dependent variables, only around a third of the variance could be attributed to stable personality, sociodemographic characteristics, or traits (between .22 and .39).
Multilevel modeling was deemed appropriate.
Hypothesis 1 tested the positive within-person association of informality with its striving potential at the situation level.

Looking at fixed within-effects, communication episodes being more informal than usual for employees were positively and significantly associated with a communication episode's striving potential (b = .23, SE = .09, p = .016).
As the model with random intercepts and slopes converged, random effects could be observed.

There was substantial between-person variability in striving potential (random intercept variance τ₀₀ = 0.34) and heterogeneity in the within-person effect of informality (random slope variance τ₁₁ = 0.03), indicating that the within-person effect differed across individuals.
The fixed effects explained 19.6% of the variance in striving potential (marginal R² = .196), whereas the full multilevel model, including random effects, explained 52.0% (conditional R² = .520).
To conclude, Hypothesis 1 was supported by the present data.
Hypothesis 2 tested whether the striving potential of the informal communication episode would be positively associated with relatedness need satisfaction within persons.

Fixed effects estimates showed that a higher striving potential than usual was significantly and positively associated with relatedness need satisfaction at the situation level (b = .67, SE = .11, p = .000).
The data were therefore consistent with H2.
Hypothesis 3 tested whether striving potential positively predicted social energy expenditure within persons.
Results showed that episodes with higher-than-usual striving potential were not significantly associated with social energy expenditure (b = -.28, SE = 0.15, p = .055).
Therefore, H3 was rejected.
Hypothesis 4 asked how striving potential was associated with a relatedness-to-energy ratio of a communication episode.
Results showed that episodes with higher-than-usual striving potential were positively and significantly associated with a higher-than-usual relatedness-to-energy ratio (b = .39, SE = .11, p = .001).
This means that if employees had a social interaction with more striving qualities, the benefits of their encounter more strongly outweighed the energy-related costs.
H4 was accepted.

Finally, RQ1 asked whether and how modality (i.e., text vs. audio vs. audiovisual vs. faceto-face) would interact with the striving potential of the communication episode within persons in association with (a) relatedness need satisfaction and (b) social energy expenditure, and (c) the relatedness-to-energy ratio.
To obtain results, all models explaining relatedness, energy expenditure, or the relatedness-to-energy-ratio included a moderation term for striving potential and modality.
Results showed no significant interaction effects, but significant simple effects for modality conditions, with audiovisual as the reference category.

Compared with audiovisual interactions, text-based interactions were associated with significantly lower levels of energy expenditure (b = -1.08, SE = 0.24, p = .000) and a significantly higher relatedness-to-energy ratio (b = 0.37, SE = .18, p = .043), holding other predictors constant.

Furthermore, relative to audiovisual modality, face-to-face showed a significant increase in relatedness need satisfaction (b = 0.59, SE = .23, p = .011) and a relative decrease in energy expenditure (b = -0.93, SE = .30, p = .002). 5 However, as the prevalence of face-to-face interaction was comparably low in the sample, these results must be interpreted with caution.

text.text: This study advances conceptual and methodological debates on the well-being function of informal communication in hybrid work.

Conceptually, prior work leaves unclear whether and by which mechanism digital informal communication confers the same benefits as face-toface, given that informal communication is held to restore employees' resources while its digital forms are presumed to deplete them.
Methodologically, prior work has relied on proxies such as between-person differences in channel use or frequency, and so cannot assess whether a given episode restores or taxes resources.

Drawing on CBB Theory, we move beyond whether employees communicate to how a given episode unfolds and is appraised, disentangling the contributions of communication quality from channel modality across relational benefits, energy expenditure, and their ratio.
Our experience-sampling design isolates these episode-level effects from stable individual differences, a distinction prior work could not draw.
Given these improvements over prior research, our results showed that informal communication is a positive experience on average, beneficial for employees' well-being.

It retains its relational benefits as long as it is pleasant, deep, meaningful, and self-disclosing (H1) -even when it takes place in the work context, requires energy at the same time (H4), or occurs via more demanding modalities prevalent in hybrid work (RQ1).

On the one hand, the positive contribution of informal communication to well-being primarily builds on the positive association of informal communication with quality characteristics of communication episodes.

When social interactions with co-workers or supervisors were perceived as more informal than usual, they were also more meaningful, pleasant, deep, self-disclosing, and personal, representing core characteristics of CBB Theory's striving potential.
On the other hand, informal communication with more-than-usual striving characteristics also satisfied relatedness needs more than usual.

Support for these associations evidences key propositions of CBB Theory: it empirically links striving attributes to CBB Theory's proposed psychological benefits of striving communication, by showing that relatedness needs are satisfied in a situation.
Higher feelings of relatedness are then a "proximal indicator of the need to belong being satiated" (Hall and Davis, 2017, p. 39).

text.text: Contrary to the association between striving potential and the satisfaction of relatedness needs, striving potential was not significantly related to social energy expenditure within persons.

Episodes with higher levels of meaningfulness or self-disclosure than usual, for instance, were not more energy-depleting. Hall and Davis (2017) note that the degree of energy expenditure is also "a function of familiarity with the behaviour, episode, person, and context" (p. 34).

text.text: Similar to the hidden contingencies above, energy expenditure may be explained by the extent to which informal communication is routine for employees, by the relationship with the communication partner beyond the hierarchical level, or by contextual variables (e.g., time of day or prior social contact).
In daily work life, employees' capacity for informal interaction may fluctuate with workload and the amount of formal communication scheduled during the day.

text.text: Interestingly, the results showed heterogeneity in the association between informality of communication episodes and their striving potential, suggesting hidden moderators.

Possible moderators could be drawn from the definition components in Singh and Denner (2025), such as actors (e.g., their relationship, their physical proximity) or the situation (e.g., the degree of volition, current workload, time of day, communication norms and culture within the organization) (for overviews, see also Begemann et al., 2024; Methot et al., 2026).

text.text: This heterogeneity may also reflect distinct forms of informal communication with different functions.

Methot and colleagues' (2026) circumplex model, for instance, distinguishes discrete forms varying in valence and depth -from superficial-positive talk like small talk to substantive-positive talk like meaningful conversation, which may differ in striving potential.

While most episodes in our data carried striving qualities, this diversity makes the heterogeneity plausible and calls for differentiating, in future studies, between routine, superficial informal talk with a comparatively favourable relatedness-to-energy ratio and more effortful, meaningful informal talk that consumes greater energy.

Moderation analyses further revealed that striving potential and modality did not interact with relatedness, social energy expenditure, or the relatedness-to-energy ratio, which means that the relatedness benefits of communication quality are not dependent on whether informal talk occurred face-to-face, via text, via audio, or audiovisually.
This is more consistent with adaptation-based accounts (Social Information Processing Theory; Walther, 1992) than with the cues-filtered-out paradigm (Daft and Lengel, 1986).

text.text: However, significant simple effects of the modality condition, text vs. audiovisual, on both outcomes have insightful implications for informal communication: When employees had a text encounter with a co-worker rather than an audiovisual one, they perceived the communication episode as less energy-consuming.
This result supports the view that video-conferencing can be particularly energy-depleting (e.g., "Zoom Fatigue"; Bailenson, 2021).

For interpersonal and organizational researchers as well as CMC scholars, this study extends CBB Theory by investigating part of its proposed mechanisms in a hybrid work context, where participants are also sometimes obliged to communicate more or less than preferred (Hall, 2018; Hall et al., 2021; Hall and Davis, 2017).

text.text: In this regard, we may rethink the role of the workplace in CBB Theory.

It has primarily treated work as a context that reshapes and often even constrains social self-regulation because workplace obligations displace optimal social contact in terms of close tie interaction, energy conservation, and relatedness needs (Hall and Davis, 2017).
