text.text: In addition, work talk is routine, non-volitional, and thus akin to "empty social calories" (Hall, 2018; Hall et al., 2021).

text.text: This complicates CBB Theory's implied dual route, in which striving typically flows from close ties but not from instrumental talk with weak ties.
Relationships to co-workers typically occupy the space between (Fingerman et al., 2025), affording relatedness-beneficial communication despite an exchange context governed by professional norms.

text.text: What ultimately distinguishes the workplace, from a CBB perspective, is that relational and formal communication compete, sometimes within the same relationships and interactions.
An informal striving episode at work is thus relationship-forming talk accomplished within a formal field densely filled with impediments to energy and relatedness management.

That such episodes nonetheless carry striving potential indicates that the CBB mechanism has more scope than prior work assumed: belonging can be assembled episode by episode, even within an obligation-dense context and across modalities.

Plausibly, a formal, instrumental backdrop even heightens the perceived relatedness of striving exchanges, making episodes considered informal within an organization stand out more than they would in a purely social setting.
This interpretation awaits empirical test, but makes concrete a suggestion in CBB Theory: that context reshapes striving (Hall and Davis, 2017).

text.text: For communication managers, our findings translate into three concrete recommendations: First, actively recognizing the well-being benefits of informal communication, as it is an important gateway to job satisfaction, employee health, and well-being ("the happy-productive worker" thesis; Fang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For communication managers, our findings translate into three concrete recommendations: First, actively recognizing the well-being benefits of informal communication, as it is an important gateway to job satisfaction, employee health, and well-being ("the happy-productive worker" thesis; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In practice, this means protecting informal exchange rather than treating it as time off-task.
Second, create opportunities for unforced, authentic exchange among co-workers, e.g., by open recreational spaces offline or dedicated informal channels online.

Because informal communication showed relational benefit which proved largely independent of channel modality, these should apply across in-office, remote, and hybrid settings and must be deliberately enabled.
Employees, particularly during onboarding, need organizational support for this initiation.
Our study thus suggests caution in treating face-to-face as a "gold standard" requiring employees to "come back to the office" at all costs.
Third, balance such opportunities against employees' limited energy, as modalities differ in the effort they require.

For instance, fewer mandatory meetings or video-conferences can protect the resources that meaningful informal exchange depends on, whereas text-based channels have a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio and may thus aid employees to balance multiple demands during their workday.
Even though this is the first study to investigate informal communication and well-being in hybrid work from a situational perspective, some caveats need to be acknowledged.
First, the small sample size was sufficient for the preregistered within-person tests (Arend and Schäfer, 2019; see methods section) but did not permit robust estimation of between-person effects.

text.text: Our within-person sample was also somewhat smaller than comparable studies, so results should be interpreted cautiously and replicated with larger samples.
Future studies should adopt broader recruitment, such as partnering with organizations or panel providers.
Additionally, compliance was reduced by challenges inherent to ESM in employee samples, as prompts may interrupt work tasks or meetings, leading participants to silence devices and miss surveys.
To mitigate this, we recommend multimodal prompting (e.g., smartphone plus desktop).
Second, we relied on single items from prior work, which are indispensable in situ but warrant systematic validation.

Organizations now navigate the back-tooffice movement alongside concerns about a "loneliness epidemic" that also affects relationships at work.

In this context, the present study examines the mechanisms of the well-being function of informal communication in everyday hybrid work, advancing understanding of its functional role for employees and organizations (Denner et al., 2025).

text.text: We show that informal communication can support high-quality exchanges among co-workers and thus employee well-being.
Yet digital communication may not be uniformly beneficial, as high-bandwidth formats, in particular, also draw on employees' limited social energy.
Informal communication should thus emphasize its recreational function and not be a further source of strain.

Continued longitudinal and situational research is crucial to understand how employees navigate a world of permanent digital connectedness while remaining healthy and engaged -an ongoing issue for social scientists, communication managers, and public health advocates alike.

While necessary given the limited literature at the time, this may have introduced heterogeneity in what participants counted as informal.
Future work should test whether a shared definition sharpens measurement without increasing burden.
Similarly, participants reported the main modality of their most recent interaction, although workplace communication is often multimodal (McEwan, 2021).
Rapid modality shifts (e.g., voice memo followed by text within a messenger) may be difficult to recall.
Still, the present ESM design reduces recall bias compared to cross-sectional survey designs and provides a step toward understanding informal communication in daily work contexts.
More granular results may be obtained by behavior observation or tracking.
Third, the study could not fully address several contingencies and temporal self-regulation dynamics emphasized in informal communication research and CBB Theory.

It offers limited insight into sociodemographic factors, traits, and job characteristics, although the withinperson design controlled for stable individual differences and ICCs indicated small betweenperson variance.
Still, the sample overrepresented younger, highly educated white-collar employees.
Given potential age-related differences in technological competence, older employees may experience digital informal communication as more energy-taxing, for instance.

Future research should use more diverse samples, examine situational boundary conditions, and could trace CBB Theory's self-regulatory dynamics through sequential, causal analyses of episodes across workdays.
